title: Classes and RAII
description: Encapsulation, constructors/destructors, and the killer C++ idiom

concepts.title: C++ Is C With Classes (Plus a Lot More)
concepts.contentHtml:
C++, designed by Bjarne Stroustrup starting in 1979, began as "C with Classes" — adding object-oriented programming to C while preserving its low-level control. Forty-five years later, C++ has grown into a multi-paradigm language with templates, exceptions, lambdas, concepts, modules, and more.

The language remains largely backward-compatible with C. Most C code compiles as C++. This compatibility is both a feature (immediate access to vast existing C codebases) and a curse (C's footguns persist). Modern C++ (C++11 and later) provides safer abstractions, but the old, raw-pointer-and-manual-malloc style still works.

The language is famously massive. The C++ standard is over 1500 pages. Few developers know all of it. Effective C++ practice is about choosing a tasteful subset, sticking to modern idioms, and avoiding the corners that trap the unwary. Scott Meyers' books, Stroustrup's own "A Tour of C++," and the C++ Core Guidelines distill what to use and what to avoid.

concepts.title: Constructors, Destructors, and the Rule of 0/3/5
concepts.contentHtml:
A C++ class bundles state and behavior. Special constructors initialize objects; the destructor runs when an object goes out of scope. The compiler can synthesize default versions, but explicit ones are needed when the class manages a resource.

The classic guideline is the Rule of Three: if you write any of {destructor, copy constructor, copy assignment operator}, you probably need all three. Modern C++ adds the Rule of Five (also move constructor and move assignment) and the Rule of Zero (use member types that handle resources for you, so you write none of the special members).

The Rule of Zero is the modern best practice. Use std::vector instead of raw arrays, std::unique_ptr instead of raw pointers, std::string instead of char arrays. Each of those types correctly implements all five special members. Your class then uses the synthesized defaults — no manual memory management code at all.
mathExpressions: \text{Rule of 0/3/5: zero special members preferred, else write all 3 (or 5)}

concepts.title: RAII: Resource Acquisition Is Initialization
concepts.contentHtml:
RAII is C++'s most important idiom. The pattern: tie a resource (memory, file handle, lock, network connection) to an object's lifetime. Acquire the resource in the constructor; release it in the destructor. When the object goes out of scope, cleanup happens automatically.

This is dramatically better than manual cleanup. std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(m); acquires the lock; the destructor releases it on scope exit, even if an exception is thrown. std::ifstream f("data.txt"); opens the file; closing happens automatically. std::unique_ptr<Foo> p(new Foo); manages heap memory; delete happens automatically.

RAII solves what manual cleanup could not: exception safety. With manual cleanup(); calls, an exception between acquire and cleanup leaks the resource. With RAII, the destructor runs as the exception unwinds the stack. RAII is why modern C++ can safely use exceptions without the resource leaks that plague Java/C# without try-with-resources.

title: Templates and Generic Programming
description: Compile-time code generation and type-parameterized algorithms

concepts.title: Function and Class Templates
concepts.contentHtml:
Templates are C++'s answer to generic programming. template <typename T> T max(T a, T b) { return a > b ? a : b; } defines a function that works for any type T supporting >. The compiler generates a separate version for each T you call it with — max(3, 5) produces an int version; max(3.0, 5.0) produces a double version.

Class templates work the same way: template <typename T> class vector { ... };. vector<int> and vector<string> are distinct types generated from the same template. The Standard Template Library (STL) uses class templates extensively for containers and algorithms.

Templates are resolved at compile time — the generated code is as fast as if you'd hand-written it. There's no runtime overhead like Java's type erasure or Python's duck typing. The cost: longer compile times, larger binaries (multiple instantiations), and notoriously cryptic error messages when things go wrong. C++20's concepts finally let you constrain template parameters, dramatically improving error messages.
mathExpressions: \text{template instantiation: code generated per type at compile time}

concepts.title: Template Specialization and SFINAE
concepts.contentHtml:
Templates can be specialized for specific types. template <> class vector<bool> { ... } defines a special vector-of-bool that packs bits to save space (a famously controversial choice). Specialization lets you optimize for known cases while keeping the generic version.

Templates also support partial specialization for class templates: providing a more specific implementation for, say, all pointer types or all maps with int keys. This is the foundation of much template metaprogramming.

The advanced trick is SFINAE (Substitution Failure Is Not An Error): if substituting template arguments produces an invalid type, the compiler removes that overload from consideration rather than erroring. Library writers used SFINAE for type traits, conditional dispatch, and detecting features. C++20 concepts replace much SFINAE with cleaner syntax: template <std::integral T> T add(T a, T b); says T must satisfy the integral concept.
mathExpressions: \text{SFINAE: substitution failure} \to \text{remove from overload set, not error}

concepts.title: constexpr and Compile-Time Computation
concepts.contentHtml:
C++ has gradually expanded what can be computed at compile time. constexpr functions can be evaluated at compile time when called with constant arguments. constexpr int factorial(int n) { return n <= 1 ? 1 : n * factorial(n-1); } can produce factorial(5) = 120 entirely at compile time, baking the result into the binary.

Each C++ standard expanded constexpr's reach. C++11 allowed simple expressions; C++14 added loops and locals; C++17 added if constexpr for compile-time branching; C++20 allowed allocations, virtual functions, and even std::vector in constexpr contexts. C++23 adds constexpr to most of the standard library.

This blurs the line between runtime and compile time. Sophisticated libraries use compile-time computation for size calculations, validation, and metaprogramming. The downside: extreme constexpr code can be slow to compile and produce mysterious errors. The trend is real and useful, but it's also the kind of feature that's easy to over-apply.
mathExpressions: \text{constexpr: function callable at compile time when given constexpr args}

title: Move Semantics and Smart Pointers
description: Avoiding copies, transferring ownership, and managing memory safely

concepts.title: lvalues, rvalues, and References
concepts.contentHtml:
C++11 introduced rvalue references (T&&) to enable move semantics. The vocabulary: an lvalue has identity and persists (a named variable); an rvalue is temporary (the result of an expression). T& is an lvalue reference; T&& is an rvalue reference.

The key insight: when an object is about to be destroyed, you can steal its resources rather than copying them. std::string s = std::move(other); transfers other's internal buffer into s instead of copying the characters. other is left in a valid-but-unspecified state.

This matters enormously for performance. Returning a large vector from a function used to copy it; with move semantics, the return value is moved (or even better, eliminated entirely via copy elision). The whole STL was retrofitted to support moves. Modern C++ code is dramatically faster than C++03 code on many workloads, mostly because of this single feature.

concepts.title: unique_ptr, shared_ptr, weak_ptr
concepts.contentHtml:
Modern C++ avoids raw new/delete. The standard library's smart pointers handle the lifetime for you.

std::unique_ptr<T>: exclusive ownership. Cannot be copied (only moved). When it goes out of scope, the pointee is deleted. Replaces 99% of raw pointer ownership in modern C++. Zero overhead — same size and speed as a raw pointer.

std::shared_ptr<T>: shared ownership via reference counting. The pointee is deleted when the last shared_ptr to it is destroyed. Useful for graphs and caches where multiple owners exist. Has overhead: an atomic counter per object.

std::weak_ptr<T>: a non-owning observer of a shared_ptr. Doesn't keep the pointee alive but can be 'locked' to obtain a shared_ptr if it's still valid. Used to break shared_ptr cycles (parent owns child via shared, child observes parent via weak — otherwise neither is freed).

concepts.title: Move-Only Types and the End of new/delete
concepts.contentHtml:
Smart pointers and move semantics enable move-only types: classes that can be moved but not copied. std::unique_ptr, std::thread, std::ifstream are all move-only. This makes single ownership enforced by the type system rather than convention.

The pattern: when ownership matters and copying makes no sense (a thread, a file handle, an exclusive resource), make the type move-only. Functions take it by rvalue reference or by value with a move at the call site. Compilation will catch any accidental copy attempt.

Modern C++ best practice: raw new and delete belong nowhere in application code. Use std::make_unique<T>(args...) or std::make_shared<T>(args...) for heap allocation. Use std::vector, std::string, std::array for collections. The C-style memory management still works for compatibility, but in clean modern code, you should never see delete outside of low-level libraries.

title: The STL: Containers, Iterators, Algorithms
description: C++'s remarkable generic library and how to wield it

concepts.title: Containers: vector, map, unordered_map, and Friends
concepts.contentHtml:
The STL containers are template classes for common data structures. std::vector<T>: dynamic array, by far the most-used container. std::array<T, N>: fixed-size array. std::deque<T>: double-ended queue. std::list<T>: doubly linked list (rarely the right choice).

Associative containers: std::map<K, V> (sorted, typically red-black tree, O(log n)), std::unordered_map<K, V> (hash table, O(1) average), and the set versions of each. There are also multi- variants that allow duplicate keys.

The default rule: use std::vector unless you have a specific reason not to. Cache locality wins over linked-list theory in practice. Use unordered_map for hash-based lookups. Avoid std::list in nearly all real code.
mathExpressions: \text{default = std::vector} \quad \text{(cache wins over Big-O for small to medium n)}

concepts.title: Iterators and Algorithms
concepts.contentHtml:
STL algorithms work on any container via iterators. std::sort(v.begin(), v.end()); sorts a vector. The same std::sort works on arrays, deques, custom containers — anything that exposes random-access iterators.

The library is huge: find, count, copy, transform, accumulate, partition, unique, rotate, shuffle, min_element, max_element, binary_search, lower_bound. Each works through iterator pairs (begin, end) or now via ranges (C++20).

The 2020 ranges library lets you compose pipelines: auto evens = vec | std::views::filter(is_even) | std::views::transform(square) | std::views::take(10);. Lazy evaluation, no intermediate containers, dramatically more readable than the equivalent iterator-pair calls. C++23 expands ranges further. This is one area where modern C++ feels like Haskell or Rust.

concepts.title: Lambdas and Functional Style
concepts.contentHtml:
C++11 introduced lambda expressions: [capture](args) { body }. They create anonymous function objects, perfect for STL algorithms: std::sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int a, int b) { return a > b; }); sorts in descending order.

The capture clause controls how lambdas access outer variables. [] captures nothing; [x] captures x by value; [&x] by reference; [=] all by value; [&] all by reference. C++14 added init captures: [ptr = std::move(orig)] moves into the lambda.

Lambdas turned C++ into a much more functional language. Combined with std::function (type-erased callable) and ranges, much code that used to require a separate functor class becomes a one-liner. Performance is excellent: lambdas are just classes with an operator(), fully inlined when possible. Modern STL is unimaginable without them.

title: Modern C++: 11/14/17/20/23
description: How the language has transformed in the last decade

concepts.title: C++11/14: The Modernization
concepts.contentHtml:
C++11 was a watershed: auto type deduction, range-based for loops, lambdas, smart pointers, move semantics, nullptr, threading library, constexpr, uniform initialization, variadic templates. The language went from clunky to genuinely pleasant for a huge fraction of code.

C++14 was a refinement: generic lambdas, return type deduction, more constexpr, std::make_unique. C++17 added structured bindings (auto [k, v] = pair;), std::optional, std::variant, std::filesystem, and parallel algorithms.

By C++17, the language had caught up to peer languages on safety and ergonomics. The Rule of Zero became practical, exception-safe code became natural, the standard library covered most domains. Modern C++17 code looks more like high-level languages than C — auto, range-for, lambdas, smart pointers everywhere.
mathExpressions: C++11: \text{auto, lambda, smart ptrs, move, threads, constexpr}

concepts.title: C++20: Concepts, Ranges, Modules, Coroutines
concepts.contentHtml:
C++20 shipped four big features. Concepts: constrain templates with named requirements (std::integral, std::sortable, your own). Compile errors finally make sense.

Ranges: lazy view pipelines over containers. vec | filter(...) | transform(...). Composable, readable, often as fast as hand-written loops. Modules: a real module system replacing the include-everything-everywhere C model. Faster compiles, no header guard fights. Adoption has been slower than hoped due to tooling/build-system support.

Coroutines: stackless coroutines for async code. co_await, co_yield, co_return turn functions into coroutines. The standard library's coroutine support is sparse; libraries like cppcoro and folly::coro fill the gap. C++20 coroutines are powerful but the API surface area is large.

concepts.title: C++23 and Beyond: Where the Language Is Going
concepts.contentHtml:
C++23's biggest features: std::expected (Rust-style Result type for error handling), std::print (modern formatted output replacing iostreams), multidimensional subscript, deducing this, more constexpr. The standard library continues catching up to user demands.

The bigger picture: C++ is increasingly competing with Rust for systems programming. Major efforts are underway to address the safety gap. Profiles (proposed for C++26) would offer a 'safe subset' of the language, banning the most common UB sources. The Carbon language (Google) and Cpp2/cppfront (Herb Sutter) explore C++-compatible successor languages with stricter defaults.

The brute reality: C++ has 50 billion lines of legacy code and ABI commitments that make rapid evolution painful. Modern C++ is a beautiful language for a thoughtful subset, but the language as a whole is enormous and hostile to newcomers. Whether C++ remains dominant in the 2030s or yields to Rust depends largely on whether 'safe by default' actually arrives in the language itself.
